holding_summary: An agreement to let an apartment-hotel suite for $70 per week inclusive of board for a family did not create an ordinary landlord-tenant relationship, because the furnishing of board was a substantial, not merely incidental, part of the consideration. On the tenant's breach, the landlord's recoverable damages were limited to the contract price less the cost she would have incurred furnishing the board, not the full rent.

The marital relationship raised a presumption that the board and lodging she furnished him in the boarding house she operated were gratuitous, not for hire.

holding_summary: New York's lien law gives keepers of hotels, boarding houses, and lodging houses a statutory lien on a boarder's or lodger's property for proper charges due for accommodation, board, and lodging. Because the respondent failed to prove that the $600 owed to her by the decedent was specifically for board and lodging charges rather than some other debt, the court held she had no valid lien and ordered the decedent's property turned over to the estate's administrator.

holding_summary: A woman who resided in a hotel annex for seventeen months, moved substantial personal property including a piano into her rooms, and dealt directly with the proprietors rather than hotel staff was not a transient 'guest' for purposes of the innkeeper's strict insurer liability, even though no fixed lodging term was ever agreed and she changed rooms several times. Because the relationship of innkeeper and guest did not exist, her complaint for loss of property was dismissed.

A woman, who had lived for 17 months in an inn which accommodated both transient and permanent lodgers, and had moved property into her rooms, which indicated an intention to make more than a temporary sojourn, and had made the arrangements for her stay with the proprietors themselves, instead of the clerk, was not a traveler and guest, within the rule which makes an innkeeper an insurer of the property of his guest, although, when she first went to the inn, she contemplated housekeeping, and never made any agreement for lodging for a definite time, and had frequently changed her apartments during her stay at the inn.
